article.headline: Citi's Fifteen Rules for Surviving the Semiconductor Cycle
article.lede: A compact set of institutional heuristics for semiconductor investing — attributed to Citigroup's long-tenured chip analyst — has one rule above all others: buy when component delivery times are lengthening, sell when they begin to shrink. As of mid-2026, multiple data sources confirm the signal is firmly in buy territory.
article.body:
A research document published by Citigroup (C) — known informally as the '15 Axioms of Semiconductor Investing' and widely attributed to the bank's long-tenured semiconductor equity analyst Christopher Danely — has circulated among institutional fund managers as a compact taxonomy of how chip stocks actually behave. The rules are blunt by design, shaped by decades of boom-and-bust *semiconductor cycles*: don't rely on management to call a downturn, don't buy on valuation, and never assume 'it's different this time.' Distributed to institutional clients through Citi's proprietary research platform, the document is not publicly indexed; its axioms circulate on financial social media as a kind of informal catechism.

Axiom seven — 'buy stocks when lead times go out, sell stocks when lead times come in' — is the most actionable of the fifteen. **Lead times** are the elapsed weeks between placing a component order and receiving it. When customers must book further in advance, it signals that fabrication capacity is being strained by demand. That strain generates a feedback loop: procurement managers place duplicate orders with multiple suppliers as insurance, a phenomenon called *double-ordering*, which artificially inflates apparent demand and accelerates price increases. Chip company earnings revisions follow one or two quarters later, and stocks — which discount future earnings — typically begin moving before revenue data prints.

The current data is unambiguous. A Baird survey published in April 2026 found lead times surging across major semiconductor categories: *DRAM* (dynamic random-access memory, the dominant form of computer working memory) has stretched to 41 weeks for DDR5 and mobile variants; Xilinx-branded *FPGAs* — reconfigurable logic chips now part of Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) — are quoted at 40 weeks; microcontrollers from STMicroelectronics (STM) are running 55 weeks or longer in some distribution channels. Component distributor Sourceability noted that supply-chain inventory buffers had collapsed from 31 weeks to under eight. Micron Technology (MU) has reportedly sold out its entire 2026 allocation of *high-bandwidth memory* (HBM), the stacked-memory architecture that AI accelerators require in volume.

The macro context reinforces the signal. The Semiconductor Industry Association reported global chip sales of $791.7 billion in 2025 — a record, up 25.6% year-on-year — with the industry on track to breach $1 trillion in 2026. Deloitte estimated that AI-specific chips will account for roughly half of all semiconductor revenue that year, driven by demand for accelerators and HBM from *hyperscaler* data-centre operators. A KPMG confidence survey reached its third-highest reading in two decades at the end of 2025, with 93% of industry leaders expecting further revenue growth.

The remaining fourteen axioms function as guardrails rather than entry signals. The list is sceptical of management guidance (axioms two and ten), dismissive of valuation-based trades (axiom one), and pessimistic about corporate pivots away from core businesses (axiom twelve). Axiom thirteen — second-tier companies feel downturns earliest and recover latest — is an asymmetry worth keeping in mind as the upcycle draws attention to smaller names. Axiom fifteen instructs investors to pause when a stock stops reacting rationally to news, a behavioural warning that sentiment has disconnected from fundamentals in either direction. None are novel observations; the document's value lies in assembling them, unadorned, as a single checklist.

concepts.definition: The recurring boom-and-bust pattern in chip industry revenue, typically spanning four to five years. It is driven by the multi-year lag between demand signals and new fabrication capacity coming online, which produces alternating periods of shortage and glut. Semiconductor stocks tend to lead the revenue cycle by one to two quarters.

The elapsed time between placing a purchase order with a chip manufacturer or distributor and receiving the components. In normal conditions this runs eight to sixteen weeks; during supply crunches it can exceed fifty weeks. Expanding lead times signal demand outpacing supply capacity; contracting lead times signal the reverse.

The practice of placing duplicate purchase orders with multiple chip suppliers simultaneously, typically as insurance when shortages are feared. It inflates apparent industry demand beyond real end-market consumption and can cause severe inventory gluts when the shortage resolves and excess orders are cancelled.

Dynamic random-access memory — the dominant form of volatile working memory in computers, servers, and smartphones. Unlike flash storage, it must be constantly refreshed with electrical charge to retain data. The primary producers are Micron Technology, SK Hynix, and Samsung.

Field-programmable gate array — a semiconductor chip whose logic circuits can be reconfigured by the buyer after manufacture, unlike fixed-function chips such as CPUs or GPUs. FPGAs are used in telecommunications infrastructure, aerospace, and increasingly in AI inference workloads where hardware flexibility matters more than raw throughput.

A type of DRAM in which multiple memory dies are stacked vertically and connected directly to a processor or accelerator via a very wide data interface. It delivers far higher data-transfer rates than conventional DRAM at lower power and is essential for AI accelerators such as Nvidia's H100 and B200 series.

A company that operates data centres at the largest scale — typically Amazon, Microsoft, Google, and Meta — and spends tens of billions of dollars annually on server infrastructure including custom and third-party AI chips. Hyperscaler capital-expenditure cycles have become a primary driver of semiconductor demand in the 2020s.

ticker_amd.name: Advanced Micro Devices, Inc.
ticker_amd.blurb: AMD is a fabless semiconductor company that designs CPUs (EPYC for data centres, Ryzen for consumer PCs) and GPUs (Instinct for AI/HPC, Radeon for gaming and workstations). Under CEO Lisa Su, AMD has taken significant data-centre CPU market share from Intel with its EPYC server processors, which now command an estimated 30%+ of the x86 server CPU market. AMD's MI300X and MI350 AI accelerators compete directly with NVIDIA's H100/H200 family and are gaining traction with hyperscalers seeking GPU supply alternatives. All AMD chips are manufactured by TSMC.
ticker_amd.recent: AMD reported strong 2025 revenue growth led by EPYC and Instinct, with data-centre revenue crossing $12 billion annually. Forward P/E of ~32.6x on 63.8% projected EPS growth yields a PEG of 0.51 — compelling for a company with clear data-centre CPU momentum and an AI accelerator portfolio that is gaining customer adoption. NVIDIA's dominant CUDA ecosystem remains the primary competitive barrier for AMD's GPU ambitions.

ticker_stm.name: STMicroelectronics N.V.
ticker_stm.blurb: STMicroelectronics is a global semiconductor group covering microcontrollers, sensors (MEMS), and — most relevant to the AI power-plumbing thesis — a broad power-semiconductor portfolio spanning SiC MOSFETs (STPOWER Gen 4), GaN devices, silicon IGBTs, and power-management ICs. ST is one of only a handful of vendors with an end-to-end 800 VDC power-conversion solution for AI data centres, offering complete reference designs from 800V bus-to-50V, 12V, and 6V conversion using its own SiC and GaN silicon. The company serves automotive, industrial, and, increasingly, hyperscale data-centre customers.
ticker_stm.recent: ST reported Q1 2026 revenue of $3.10 billion, up 23% year-over-year and above consensus of $3.04 billion, with Q2 2026 guidance of ~$3.45 billion. In March 2026 the company announced expanded 800 VDC power-conversion products (12V and 6V architectures) developed to the NVIDIA 800 VDC reference design and showcased at NVIDIA GTC 2026. In February 2026 ST disclosed a multi-year, multi-billion-dollar engagement with Amazon Web Services to supply semiconductors for AWS compute and AI data-centre infrastructure. Management projects data-centre revenue exceeding $500 million in 2026 and surpassing $1 billion in 2027.

ticker_mu.name: Micron Technology, Inc.
ticker_mu.blurb: Micron is the only US-headquartered manufacturer of DRAM and NAND memory at scale, competing with Samsung and SK Hynix. Historically the most cyclical of the three, it has spent the past two years repositioning toward high-bandwidth memory (HBM), the stacked DRAM that pairs with AI accelerators, where pricing is multiples of standard DDR5 and contracts are multi-year rather than spot.
ticker_mu.recent: In March 2026 Micron began mass production of HBM4 12-Hi 36GB stacks for Nvidia's Vera Rubin platform; management has stated 2026 HBM capacity is sold out under binding agreements. Fiscal Q2 2026 revenue was around $23.9 billion, with non-GAAP gross margin near 75%. The board approved a 30% dividend increase and roughly $25 billion of fiscal-2026 capex. Despite a strong year-to-date move, the forward P/E remains in the high single digits on consensus, reflecting residual cyclicality scepticism.
